kurals.tamil:
கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்
ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள.
kurals.transliteration:
Kandukettu unduyirththu utrariyum aimpulanum
ondhodi kanne ula.
kurals.meaning: All the joys that the five senses know, by seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching, are found together in this one woman with bright bangles.
kurals.elementary: Think of the best day of a holiday: you see the lights, hear the music, taste the sweets, smell the flowers and feel a warm hug. Usually each good thing comes from a different place. The lover in this verse says that, for him, every one of those good feelings comes from one single person he loves.
kurals.university: Chapter 111 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on premarital, secret love) and follows the exchange of glances in ch. 110; in the commentary tradition that runs through Parimelazhagar it voices the hero’s (talaivan’s) joy after the lovers’ first union, and nearly every couplet is his speech. The five verbs kaṇṭu (seeing), kēṭṭu (hearing), uṇṭu (eating, tasting), uyirttu (breathing in, smelling) and uṟṟu (touching) name the aimpulaṉ (ஐம்புலன், the five senses or sense-pleasures) in their classical order, and kaṇṇē uḷa means ‘are located in her’ (kaṇ as a locative). Oṇtoṭi (ஒண்தொடி, ‘she of the bright bangle’) is a standard metonymy for a young woman; the commentators on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) gloss the line as all five sense-joys being present in her alone. Pope renders: ‘All joys that senses five- sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch- can give, / In this resplendent armlets-bearing damsel live!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the sung version printed on thirukkural.net writes ஒண்டொடி, an ordinary sandhi spelling of the same word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She seems a flower whose fragrance none has tasted, / A gem uncut by workman’s tool, / A branch no desecrating hands have wasted, / Fresh honey, beautifully cool.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta describes Shakuntala by piling up images for smell, sight, touch and taste, as if every kind of sweetness were gathered in her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the lover finds the delights of all the senses summed up in one woman.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text of Ryder’s translation; the many-senses imagery matches, but the verse praises her untouched purity before any union, so the fit is partial.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices! Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.”
christianity.explanation: The bridegroom of the Song of Songs praises his bride through sight, taste and smell at once.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved alone satisfies several senses together.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close multi-sense parallel, though hearing and touch are not named.

islam.quote_or_event: “In this world, women and perfume have been made dear to me, and my comfort has been provided in prayer.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names the love of women and of fragrance as good things of this world that God made dear to him, while placing his deepest comfort in prayer.
islam.tie_back: Islam affirms, as the Kural does, that the beloved is a rightful source of delight, but it ranks prayer above all sense-joys.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it affirms delight in a wife and in scent but does not gather all five senses in her, so the match is partial.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; For sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
judaism.explanation: The lover asks to see the beloved’s face and hear her voice, because both are sweet to him.
judaism.tie_back: Sight and hearing, two of the Kural’s five senses, both find their joy in the one beloved.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; covers only two of the five senses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening suttas of the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha says he knows of no other single sight, sound, smell, taste or touch that so overpowers a man’s mind as those of a woman, and the same of a man’s for a woman.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the same five senses as the Kural and says that the beloved’s form, voice, scent, taste and touch are the strongest pull on the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees with the Kural that all five sense-delights can meet in one person, but treats this as a danger to be understood, not a joy to be celebrated.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 1.1-10, Rupadi Vagga (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as the Access to Insight and dhammatalks pages did not load for verbatim checking; the five-sense structure is a close match, while the valuation is reversed.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s lecture takes the five senses one by one (colour, sound, smell, taste, touch) and warns that passion for the objects of each sense ruins the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism shares the Kural’s map of the five senses but sees their gathering in one beloved as a snare, the opposite of the lover’s delight.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24, with 32.22-99 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the sense-by-sense scheme matches the Kural closely, but the Jain judgment is renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Aphrodite lends Hera an embroidered girdle in which every charm is woven: love, desire and the sweet persuasion that steals the wits even of the wise.
greek_mythology.explanation: The girdle gathers every power of attraction into one object, and whoever wears it becomes irresistible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise imagines every delight of love gathered into one woman.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, since the online text loaded only partly; the idea of all charms in one place fits, though the girdle is used for a trick on Zeus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I know not how I can conceive the good, if I withdraw the pleasures of taste and withdraw the pleasures of love and those of hearing and sight.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus says he cannot even imagine the good without the pleasures of taste, love, hearing and sight.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, Epicurus counts the pleasures of all the senses, including love, as part of the good.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, quoted in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X.6 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed across several online copies of Hicks’s translation (one gives a longer variant); the senses-and-love list matches, but Epicurus is not speaking of one beloved.

kurals.tamil:
பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிறமன் அணியிழை
தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Pinikku marundhu piraman aniyizhai
thannoikkuth thaane marundhu.
kurals.meaning: For other illnesses the medicine is something different from the illness; but for the love-sickness this jewelled girl causes, she herself is the only medicine.
kurals.elementary: When you miss your best friend who has moved away, no toy or sweet makes the sad feeling go. The only thing that fixes it is seeing that friend again. The person you miss is both the reason you feel sad and the cure.
kurals.university: The couplet sets ordinary medicine against love: for a piṇi (பிணி, disease) the marundu (மருந்து, remedy) is piṟa (‘something other’), while the nōy (நோய், sickness) caused by the aṇiyiḻai (அணியிழை, ‘she of fine jewels’) is cured only by her. Man in piṟaman is an expletive particle (asai) with no meaning of its own, as the commentators note. Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the logic: remedies usually have a nature opposite to the disease, yet here the cause and the cure are the same. The idea continues ch. 110’s opening kural (1091), where one glance wounds and another heals, and moves it from the look to union itself. Pope: ‘Disease and medicine antagonists we surely see; / This maid, to pain she gives, herself is remedy.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Dear Kṛṣṇa, please pour the nectar of Your lips upon the fire within our hearts — a fire You ignited with Your smiling glances and the sweet song of Your flute.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that the burning love he lit in them by his glances and his flute can be soothed only by his own nectar.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who causes the love-sickness is the only one who can cure it.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29.35 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a near one-to-one match of cause and cure, set in devotional love for Krishna.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.”
christianity.explanation: The prophet tells Israel that the God who wounded them is the same God who will heal them.
christianity.tie_back: The pattern of the Kural, where the one who wounds is the one who heals, appears here in divine rather than human love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); the wound-and-cure structure matches, but the setting is covenant and repentance, not romance.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is nothing like marriage, for two who love one another.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that for two people who love each other, marriage is the best answer to that love.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s cure for love-sickness is the beloved herself; this hadith names lawful union with the beloved as the cure.
islam.source: Sunan Ibn Majah 1847 (graded hasan by Darussalam)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it implies the beloved is the remedy for love, though without the disease image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I kill, and I make alive; I have wounded, and I heal; And there is none that can deliver out of My hand.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Moses, God declares that wounding and healing both come from Him alone.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies to the beloved what this verse says of God: the same hand gives the wound and the healing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the structural parallel is clear but the subject is divine sovereignty, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust and no crime like hatred. There is no ill like the aggregates (of existence) and no bliss higher than the peace (of Nibbana).”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names lust as the worst fire and the peace of Nibbana as the true bliss that ends every ill.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that love is a sickness, but it places the cure in Nibbana, not in the beloved who caused it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it shares the sickness idea but rejects the Kural’s remedy, so this is a next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira traces suffering back through delusion and desire, and teaches that it ends only when desire itself ends.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also asks what cures the pain of desire, but its answer is the end of desire, not the beloved who stirred it.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it addresses the cure of desire but reverses the Kural’s answer.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telephus was wounded by Achilles’ spear, an oracle told him that only the one who had wounded him could heal him, and he was cured by rust scraped from that same spear.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this story the weapon that caused the wound is the only thing that can close it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like Achilles’ spear: the source of the wound is also its only cure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested myth, not checked verbatim this session; the wound-and-cure logic is very close, though the story is about war, not love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates says that the soul of the lover, stung and aching when apart, forgets mother, brothers and friends and holds that the beloved is the only physician of its greatest pains.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the beloved is both what wounds the lover’s soul with longing and what alone can heal it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim almost word for word: she who causes the sickness is its only medicine.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Jowett’s own summary on Project Gutenberg (‘his beloved is his physician, who can alone cure his pain’) was verified, but the dialogue text itself did not fully load.

kurals.tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்
தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar mendrol thuyilin inidhukol
thaamaraik kannaan ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Can the heaven of the lotus-eyed god be any sweeter than sleep resting on the soft shoulder of the one you love?
kurals.elementary: Imagine falling asleep safe and warm after a long trip, with someone who loves you right beside you. Grown-ups sometimes say heaven is the happiest place there is. This verse asks, with a smile, whether even heaven could feel better than that peaceful, loved feeling.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is tāmaraik kaṇṇāṉ ulagu (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு), ‘the world of the lotus-eyed one’, sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders (meṉṟōḷ) of those one loves (tām vīḻvār)? Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s line identify the lotus-eyed one with Tirumal (Vishnu) and his world with his heaven (Vaikuntha), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it this way; Kalaignar frames it as a sceptical question about what people call ‘the lotus-eyed one’s world’. The particle kol (கொல்) marks doubt, so the answer implied is ‘no’. The verse is one of the few places where the Kural names a deity by an epithet, and it ranks the joy of love above the reward of heaven only playfully, inside the love-poetry convention. Pope: ‘Than rest in her soft arms to whom the soul is giv’n, / Is any sweeter joy in his, the Lotus-eyed-one’s heaven?’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Ah, my eyes have found their heaven. Here is the darling of my thoughts, lying upon a flower-strewn bench of stone, and attended by her two friends.”
hinduism.explanation: Hidden among the branches, King Dushyanta catches sight of Shakuntala resting and says his eyes have reached heaven.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the lover calls the presence of his resting beloved a heaven in itself.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; strong on beloved-as-heaven, though it is the sight of her, not rest beside her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Songs describes resting in her beloved’s embrace.
christianity.tie_back: This is the restful embrace that the Kural says no heaven could surpass.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); the image of rest in the beloved’s arms matches, but there is no comparison with heaven.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is He who created you from one soul and created from it its mate that he might dwell in security with her.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God made the spouse so that each might find rest and security in the other.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s sweet rest on the beloved’s shoulder echoes this rest in the spouse, though Islam would never rank it above Paradise.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; matches rest in the spouse but rejects the comparison with the next world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Enjoy life with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which He hath given thee under the sun.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells the reader to take joy in life with a beloved wife as one’s portion under the sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this verse finds the sweetest portion of life in the company of the one you love, here and now.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; shares the this-worldly joy of love, without the playful comparison to heaven.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Udana, the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda longs to leave the monks for his bride, until the Buddha shows him the nymphs of the heaven of the Thirty-three, beside whom Nanda says his bride looks plain; he then stays in the order.
buddhism.explanation: The story ranks heavenly delights far above earthly love, and then teaches Nanda to give up both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural playfully ranks love above heaven; the Nanda story reverses the ranking, and Buddhism finally sets both aside.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta, not re-checked verbatim this session; the love-versus-heaven comparison is direct, but the verdict is opposite.

jainism.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that even the gods in their heavens suffer from the desire for pleasure, and only the dispassionate are free.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural weighs love against heaven and prefers love; Jainism finds both heavenly and earthly pleasure bound up with misery.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it addresses heaven’s pleasures but rejects both sides of the Kural’s comparison.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The goddess Calypso offers Odysseus immortality and ageless life if he stays with her, but he answers that though Penelope is mortal and less beautiful than a goddess, he still longs every day to go home to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus chooses life with his mortal wife over the deathless existence of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Odysseus judges the company of his own beloved sweeter than the heaven of the immortals.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene, not checked verbatim this session (the online text loaded only in part); a strong thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I have sought it, finally, because in the union of love I have seen, in a mystic miniature, the prefiguring vision of the heaven that saints and poets have imagined.”
philosophy.explanation: In the prologue to his autobiography, Bertrand Russell says the union of love gave him a glimpse of the heaven imagined by saints and poets.
philosophy.tie_back: Russell makes the Kural’s comparison directly: the joy of union rivals heaven itself.
philosophy.source: Bertrand Russell, ‘What I Have Lived For’, Prologue to The Autobiography of Bertrand Russell (1967)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed on several online copies of the prologue (some print ‘because of the union’); a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும்
தீயாண்டுப் பெற்றாள் இவள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Neengin theruum kurugungaal thannennum
theeyaandup petraal ival.
kurals.meaning: If I move away it burns me, and if I come near it cools me; where did she find such a strange fire?
kurals.elementary: Have you ever felt grumpy and hot inside when you had to leave someone you love, and calm again as soon as you were back together? The lover says she must own a magic fire: it burns when you go away and feels cool and gentle when you come close. Real fire does the opposite!
kurals.university: The conceit rests on reversing the nature of fire: ordinary fire burns those who come near and leaves those who move away, but this fire teṟūum (தெறூஉம், ‘burns’, with the vowel lengthening called uyiraḷapeṭai for metre) when he leaves (nīṅkiṉ) and taṇ eṉṉum (‘turns cool’) when he draws near (kuṟukuṅkāl). The question tī yāṇṭup peṟṟāḷ (‘from where did she get the fire?’) is wonder rather than inquiry, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) calls it a putumaiyāṉa tī, a ‘new, unheard-of fire’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that she has lit it in his heart. The couplet anticipates the separation chapters of the kaṟpiyal, where absence is described as burning. Pope: ‘Withdraw, it burns; approach, it soothes the pain; / Whence did the maid this wondrous fire obtain?’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “’Twas love that caused the burning pain; / ’Tis love that eases it again; / As when, upon a sultry day, / Rain breaks, and washes grief away.”
hinduism.explanation: Overhearing that Shakuntala’s fever comes from love for him, the king says the love that burns is the same love that brings relief like rain.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strange fire: love burns and love cools, depending on whether the lovers are apart or together.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; a close match of burning and cooling, though not tied explicitly to distance and nearness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.”
christianity.explanation: Paul advises those who burn with desire to marry, so that union quiets the burning.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, love burns when lovers are apart and is cooled by union.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); shares the burning-and-relief idea, but Paul speaks pastorally and without the Kural’s delight.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute that wails because it was cut from its reed-bed, and says that its cry is the fire of love, not mere wind.
islam.explanation: The reed’s burning lament comes from separation from its source, and only reunion would quiet it.
islam.tie_back: Rumi’s fire of separation is the Kural’s fire that burns when the lover moves away.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, opening verses (tr. R. A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as Nicholson’s text was not checked verbatim this session; strong on the burning of separation, with the beloved understood as God in Sufi reading.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs calls love a fire so fierce that no flood can put it out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too calls love a fire, though its fire has the strange gift of turning cool at the beloved’s side.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; shares love-as-fire, but not the cooling when near.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The eye is aflame. Forms are aflame... Aflame with what? Aflame with the fire of passion, the fire of aversion, the fire of delusion.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha teaches that every sense burns with passion, and that only disenchantment puts the fire out.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that passion is fire, but it cools that fire by letting go, not by drawing near to the beloved.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 35.28, Adittapariyaya Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the fire image is shared, but the remedy is the opposite of the Kural’s.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira likens the senses of an unrestrained person to a forest fire that cannot be put out.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also calls desire a fire, but holds that indulgence only feeds it, while the Kural’s lover finds it cooled by nearness.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the fire image but denies that closeness can cool it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros glukupikron, ‘sweet-bitter’, the loosener of limbs, an irresistible creature that both delights and pains the lover.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Sappho love is a single power that gives sweetness and bitterness at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s fire that both scorches and cools is the same double nature of love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known fragment, not checked against a particular translation this session; the paradox matches, though not the near-and-far pattern.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates describes the lover’s soul as throbbing and burning with pain when apart from the beloved, and finding relief from its pangs and a sweet release as soon as it sees the beloved again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the lover’s soul suffers when the beloved is absent and is soothed in the beloved’s presence.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s fire that burns at a distance and cools close by.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, since the Jowett dialogue text did not fully load for verbatim checking; the absence-pain and presence-relief pattern is a close match.

kurals.tamil:
வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே
தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள் தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vetta pozhudhin avaiyavai polume
thottaar kadhuppinaal thol.
kurals.meaning: The embrace of the girl whose hair is full of flowers gives joy just as each longed-for thing does at the very moment it is wanted.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a magic lunchbox that always holds exactly what you are hungry for: soup when you are cold, ice cream when you are hot. The lover says that being close to the one he loves is like that box: it always gives the right happiness at the right time.
kurals.university: Vēṭṭa poḻutiṉ avaiyavai pōlumē says that her shoulders (tōḷ, standing for her embrace) are ‘like each of those things at the time they are desired’: the comparison is with any object of desire enjoyed exactly when wished for. Tōṭṭār katuppiṉāḷ (தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள்) is ‘she whose tresses (katuppu) are full of petals or flowers (tōṭu)’, an epithet of the adorned beloved. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘whenever one unites with her, she gives the delight of whatever one desires’, and Kalaignar compares it to a wished-for thing arriving whenever wished; the image recalls the wish-granting tree and cow of Indian lore, though the Kural does not name them. Pope: ‘In her embrace, whose locks with flowery wreaths are bound, / Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that one who has come to know the Self moves freely in all worlds: if he desires the world of the fathers, or of mothers, or of song, or of fragrance and garlands, by his mere wish it rises up for him.
hinduism.explanation: For the knower of the Self, every desired joy appears the moment it is wished for.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the beloved this same power to supply each wished-for joy at the moment of wishing.
hinduism.source: Chandogya Upanishad 8.2.1-10 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; the ‘whatever is wished, when wished’ pattern matches, but the source is the Self, not a beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!”
christianity.explanation: The lover exclaims that the beloved is beautiful and pleasant, made for delights.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song finds every kind of delight in the beloved.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); close in spirit, without the Kural’s idea of each joy arriving at the moment it is wanted.

islam.quote_or_event: “Circulated among them will be plates and vessels of gold. And therein is whatever the souls desire and [what] delights the eyes, and you will abide therein eternally.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes Paradise as a place where every soul finds whatever it desires.
islam.tie_back: The Kural gives the beloved’s embrace this Paradise-like quality of answering every desire.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; matches ‘whatever is desired’, but describes Paradise rather than a beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the manna in the wilderness was a single food in which the Israelites could taste whatever flavour they wished, as an infant finds every taste in its mother’s milk.
judaism.explanation: One gift from heaven held every desired taste for each person who ate it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like this manna: one source that gives each longed-for sweetness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known aggadah, not checked verbatim this session; a good structural parallel in a non-romantic setting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no amount of pleasure can ever fill sensual desire.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural claims the beloved satisfies each desire as it arises; Buddhism denies that any pleasure can truly satisfy desire.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a direct counter-teaching, so only a next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira compares pleasures to a fruit that tastes delicious but turns to poison.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises a delight that answers every wish; Jainism warns that every such delight is sweet only at first.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a direct contrast rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The horn of the goat Amalthea, which nursed the infant Zeus, was said to supply meat or drink in abundance, whatever one might wish.
greek_mythology.explanation: The horn of plenty gives each person exactly what they wish for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like this horn, giving each desired joy at the moment it is wished.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.7.5, citing Pherecydes (tr. J. G. Frazer)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; the ‘whatever one wishes’ idea fits, though the horn has nothing to do with love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle teaches that friendships based on pleasure last only while the pleasure lasts, because such friends love one another not for their character but because each finds the other pleasant.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love that rests only on pleasure is the least stable kind of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural celebrates the pleasure of the beloved; Aristotle would add that lasting love needs more than pleasure.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3, 1156a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the standard Ross translation, not checked verbatim this session; it qualifies rather than echoes the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
உறுதோறு உயிர்தளிர்ப்பத் தீண்டலால் பேதைக்கு
அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Urudhoru uyirthalirppath theendalaal pedhaikku
amizhdhin iyandrana thol.
kurals.meaning: Every time I hold her, her touch makes my wilting life put out fresh shoots; this innocent girl’s shoulders must be made of nectar.
kurals.elementary: Think of a droopy plant that perks up the moment you give it water. When someone you love gives you a hug after a hard day, you can feel the same way. The lover says her hugs work like magic drink that makes him feel alive and fresh again every single time.
kurals.university: Uyir taḷirppa (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப, ‘so that life puts forth tender shoots’) is a plant image: the lover’s withered life sprouts again, as Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it (vāṭiya uyir taḷirkka, ‘the wilted life sprouting’). Uṟutōṟu means ‘every time I come close’, and from this repeated reviving effect the lover infers that her shoulders are amiḻtiṉ iyaṉṟaṉa (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன), ‘fashioned of amizhtu’, the nectar of immortality (Sanskrit amṛta). Pētai (பேதை) here means a simple, innocent young woman; it is also the name of the youngest of the seven traditional stages of womanhood, but the commentators read it in the general sense. Pope: ‘Ambrosia are the simple maiden’s arms; when I attain / Their touch, my withered life puts forth its buds again!’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a famous Rig Vedic hymn the singers declare that they have drunk the Soma and become immortal, have come to the light and found the gods.
hinduism.explanation: The sacred drink Soma, identified with amrita, is praised as giving fresh life and immortality to those who taste it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural borrows exactly this idea of a life-giving nectar to describe the beloved’s touch.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 8.48.3 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; it explains the amrita image, but the setting is ritual, not love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.”
christianity.explanation: The bride finds rest and sweetness in her beloved, like shade and fruit from a tree.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural’s lover is refreshed by the beloved’s nectar, the bride is refreshed by her beloved’s sweetness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); the refreshing sweetness matches, but there is no revival of a withered life.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet came home trembling after the first revelation, he asked Khadijah to cover him; she wrapped him, comforted him and reassured him until his fear left him.
islam.explanation: The loving presence of his wife restored the Prophet’s calm and strength at the hardest moment of his life.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, this story shows the beloved spouse’s nearness reviving a shaken spirit.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known hadith, not re-checked verbatim this session; the reviving comfort of a spouse matches, without the romantic emphasis.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted for his mother.”
judaism.explanation: Isaac, still grieving his mother, finds his grief eased by his love for Rebekah.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love for the beloved brings a drooping spirit back to life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the reviving power of love is clear, though there is no nectar image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having savored the taste of solitude and peace (of Nibbana), pain-free and stainless he becomes, drinking deep the taste of the bliss of the Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the peace of Nibbana as a taste one drinks deeply, leaving one free of pain.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism also speaks of a drink that renews life, but it finds that nectar in Nibbana, not in the beloved’s touch.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; shares the reviving-taste image but replaces the beloved with Nibbana.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira describes the liberated soul as one who has recovered from a long illness and become infinitely happy.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also speaks of life restored, but it finds that revival in liberation from desire, not in the beloved’s embrace.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the revival image is shared, but its source is the opposite of the Kural’s.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, when Zeus and Hera lie together on Mount Ida, the earth beneath them sends up fresh grass, dewy lotus, crocus and hyacinth, and a golden cloud covers them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The union of the gods makes the very ground burst into new growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels his life sprout new shoots in the embrace, as the earth blooms beneath the divine lovers.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; the sprouting image is apt, but in context Hera is beguiling Zeus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates says that when the lover gazes on beauty, warmth flows into his soul, the stiffened roots of its wings soften, and the wings begin to swell and grow again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the sight of the beloved makes the soul’s withered wings sprout anew.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image of life putting forth fresh shoots in the beloved’s presence.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Jowett’s summary (‘the stiffened wing begins to relax and grow again’) was verified on Project Gutenberg, but the dialogue text did not fully load.

kurals.tamil:
தம்மில் இருந்து தமதுபாத்து உண்டற்றால்
அம்மா அரிவை முயக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thammil irundhu thamadhupaaththu undatraal
ammaa arivai muyakku.
kurals.meaning: The embrace of this lovely, fair-skinned young woman is like living in one’s own home and eating what one has earned, after sharing it with others.
kurals.elementary: Remember how good it feels to eat a meal you helped cook, at your own table, after giving some to your friends? It feels honest and happy and safe. The lover says being close to the one he loves gives that same warm, at-home happiness.
kurals.university: The simile draws on the householder ideal of the Arattuppal: tammil iruntu (‘dwelling in one’s own home’), tamatu (‘one’s own’, i.e. what one has earned) pāttu uṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like eating after dividing and sharing it’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pāttu as distributing one’s earnings to others before eating, Solomon Pappaiah as sharing with one’s own people, and Puliyur Kesikan more narrowly as eating one’s own portion; all agree that the pleasure is one of independence, rightful ownership and generosity. Ammā is read as am (‘beautiful’) plus māmai (‘the dark-gold complexion praised in Tamil poetry’), and arivai (அரிவை) is a young woman, also the name of one of the seven traditional stages of womanhood. Muyakku (முயக்கு) is ‘embrace’. Pope: ‘As when one eats from household store, with kindly grace / Sharing his meal: such is this golden maid’s embrace.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita praises eating only after first offering the food, and condemns cooking only for oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal of eating one’s own food only after sharing it, which it uses as the measure of love’s joy, rests on this same ethic.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it matches the share-before-eating ideal, not the comparison with love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee. Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm joins the happiness of eating one’s own earnings with the blessing of a wife at home.
christianity.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural’s simile, one’s own earned food and the beloved wife, appear together in this verse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a strong match of earned food, home and wife, without the element of sharing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises food earned by one’s own work as the best food of all, citing David who lived by his own labour.
islam.tie_back: The Kural measures love’s joy by the sweetness of one’s own earned food, which this hadith calls the best meal.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; matches the earned-food half of the simile, not the love half.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink waters out of thine own cistern, And running waters out of thine own well... Let thy fountain be blessed; And have joy of the wife of thy youth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares faithful joy in one’s own wife to drinking from one’s own well.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs likens love for one’s own spouse to the satisfaction of using what is rightfully one’s own.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close structural parallel (one’s own resources and one’s own spouse), without sharing with others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the son of a good family, using the wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise... righteous wealth righteously gained, partakes of his wealth and makes merit... he experiences bliss, he experiences joy.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that a householder knows real bliss in enjoying and giving from wealth he has honestly earned.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the very pleasure the Kural uses as its measure for the joy of the beloved’s embrace.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match to the Kural’s simile, though the sutta does not mention love.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the vows of the Jain householder is atithi-samvibhaga, sharing one’s food and goods with a worthy guest or mendicant before eating oneself.
jainism.explanation: The Jain layperson is taught to divide what is his own and give a share away as a religious duty.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s picture of eating one’s own food only after sharing it reflects this same household ethic, which Jainism made a formal vow.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 7, list of lay vows (tr. Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-established vow, not checked verbatim this session, and the exact sutra number is left out because it differs between editions; it matches the simile’s sharing, not its love theme.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how the old couple Baucis and Philemon, poor but devoted to each other, share their humble meal in their own cottage with two strangers, who turn out to be Jupiter and Mercury.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their happiness lies in a loving marriage, a small home of their own and a generous table.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s simile, the joy of sharing one’s own food at home, is lived out by this loving pair.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story, not checked verbatim this session; it joins married love, one’s own home and sharing, as the Kural does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that friendship between husband and wife seems to exist by nature, includes both utility and pleasure, and that the two help each other by putting their own gifts into the common stock.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a good marriage is a partnership in which each shares what is their own.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s joy of sharing what is one’s own is, for Aristotle, built into the friendship of husband and wife.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.12, 1162a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the standard Ross translation, not checked verbatim this session; a reasonable but partial fit.

kurals.tamil:
வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே வளியிடை
போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Veezhum iruvarkku inidhe valiyidai
pozhap padaaa muyakku.
kurals.meaning: Sweet to two people who love each other is an embrace so close that not even a breath of wind can pass between them.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever hugged someone so tightly that you felt like one person? The verse says that for two people who love each other, the sweetest hug is one so close that not even a tiny puff of air could slip in between.
kurals.university: Vīḻum iruvar (வீழும் இருவர், ‘two who desire each other’) stresses that the love is mutual, and the embrace (muyakku) is one that vaḷi iṭai pōḻap paṭāa (‘is not split apart in the middle by the wind’). Paṭāa carries the metrical lengthening (aḷapeṭai) also seen in teṟūum of kural 1104. Every gloss on both sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads it as an embrace so close that even air cannot enter. Pope, characteristically, turns the image moral: ‘Sweet is the strict embrace of those whom fond affection binds, / Where no dissevering breath of discord entrance finds’, treating the wind as discord, a reading the Tamil commentators do not share. Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Now as a man, when embraced by a beloved wife, knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within, thus this person, when embraced by the intelligent (prâgña) Self, knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad uses the embrace of loving spouses, in which nothing outside or inside is felt, as an image of union with the Self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace that lets nothing come between is the same image of complete union.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Wording checked against an online copy of Max Müller’s translation (hinduwebsite.com) found by search; a strong match of complete union, used as a spiritual analogy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
christianity.explanation: Genesis says that husband and wife cling together and become one flesh.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace with no gap between the two is a picture of becoming one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong on closeness and unity, though more general than the Kural’s image.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are a clothing for you and you are a clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as garments for each other, as close as clothing to the skin.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s embrace that admits no wind, the garment image leaves nothing between the spouses.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; a close image of intimacy and closeness, within a passage on lawful marital relations.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud quotes a popular saying: loving spouses need almost no room between them, but estranged ones cannot be far enough apart.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: true lovers leave no space at all between them.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match of closeness in love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhallatiya Jataka a pair of kinnaras (forest spirits) still weep for the one night, seven hundred years earlier, when a flooded stream kept them apart.
buddhism.explanation: The couple’s love is so close that a single night’s separation is mourned for centuries, and the story leads the king to value his own wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the tale shows lovers for whom even the smallest gap is unbearable.
buddhism.source: Jataka 504, Bhallatiya Jataka (tr. ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. IV)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the story from memory of Cowell’s translation, not checked this session; a strong thematic match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But a man who is indifferent to ‘colours,’ is free from sorrows; though still in the Samsâra, he is not affected by that long succession of pains, just as the leaf of the Lotus (is not moistened) by water.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira holds up the lotus leaf, which stays untouched by the water around it, as the model of a detached soul.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises an embrace where nothing comes between; Jainism praises the opposite, a soul that nothing clings to.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; offered as a deliberate contrast, so the score is low.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Alcyone, grieving her drowned husband Ceyx, is changed into a bird together with him, and the two stay faithful mates even as birds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even transformation and death do not separate the loving pair.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers allow not even a breath of wind between them; Ceyx and Alcyone remain together beyond death.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; it matches inseparability, not the physical closeness of the image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium Aristophanes imagines Hephaestus asking two lovers lying side by side whether they wish to be wholly one, day and night in each other’s company, and offering to melt them into one and let them grow together.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristophanes, love is the longing of two halves to become one whole.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace that leaves no room even for air is the same wish to be wholly one.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of Jowett’s text, verified on Project Gutenberg; a near one-to-one match of total union.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம்
கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodal unardhal punardhal ivaikaamam
koodiyaar petra payan.
kurals.meaning: A lovers’ quarrel, making it up, and coming together again: these are the rewards that those whose love has been fulfilled enjoy.
kurals.elementary: Best friends sometimes have a small grumpy fight, then say sorry, and then feel even closer than before. The verse says that this little circle of a pretend sulk, making up and being together again is one of the sweet parts of love.
kurals.university: The couplet names the three-part movement that structures the closing chapters of the Kamattuppal: ūṭal (ஊடல், the lover’s feigned or playful sulking), uṇartal (உணர்தல், its resolution, the partner understanding and appeasing it) and puṇartal (புணர்தல், reunion). Kāmam kūṭiyār (‘those in whom love has come together’, i.e. lovers whose love is fulfilled) obtain these as payaṉ, ‘fruit’. Solomon Pappaiah places it explicitly in married life (a small tiff, reconciliation, then reunion), Puliyur Kesikan adds that the sulk should be kept within measure (aḷavōṭu), and Kalaignar gives a slightly different reading of uṇartal. The triad anticipates chapters 131-133 (Pulavi, Pulavi Nuṇukkam, Ūṭaluvakai), where the delight of the lovers’ quarrel becomes the main theme. Pope: ‘The jealous variance, the healing of the strife, reunion gained: / These are the fruits from wedded love obtained.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana Krishna teases his wife Rukmini by suggesting she would have done better to marry another king; she is so distressed that she faints, and he lifts her up, comforts her and assures her of his love, after which they are happier than before.
hinduism.explanation: A playful provocation leads to hurt, then to tender reconciliation and renewed closeness.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sequence of quarrel, making up and reunion between married lovers.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.60 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not checked verbatim this session; the tease, hurt and reconciliation pattern is a strong match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger will come but insists that it be resolved before the day ends.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul expects quarrels to be followed quickly by reconciliation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); the quarrel-then-resolve idea fits, but the verse is general, not about lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali and Fatima had a quarrel and Ali went off to sleep in the mosque; the Prophet found him lying covered in dust, brushed it off him and playfully called him ‘Abu Turab’ (father of dust), and the matter was smoothed over.
islam.explanation: A small marital quarrel is gently eased by the Prophet’s humour and affection.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ūṭal and uṇartal, this is a tiff between loving spouses that ends in reconciliation.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the hadith verified on sunnah.com; the quarrel and gentle resolution match, though the reunion itself is not described.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Songs the bride delays opening to her beloved, he turns away, and she searches for him until they are reunited and she says ‘I am my beloved’s’.
judaism.tie_back: The Song traces the Kural’s arc of estrangement, seeking and reunion between lovers.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 5:6, with 6:3 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verse 5:6 verified verbatim on Sefaria; the separation-and-reunion arc matches, though it is not presented as a playful quarrel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that hatred is never ended by hatred in this world, but only by non-hatred; this, he says, is an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Quarrels end not by answering anger with anger but by letting it go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s uṇartal, the healing of the quarrel, works by the same giving-up of resentment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse, not re-checked verbatim this session; it concerns reconciliation in general, not lovers’ play.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that attachment and aversion alike come from karma and lead to further suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural delights in love’s swing between sulking and union; Jainism sees that very swing of attraction and aversion as binding karma.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrast rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns, Penelope tests him by ordering their bed moved; he angrily protests that he built it around a living olive trunk, and this proof melts her doubt, so that they embrace in tears and go together to their old bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: A moment of testing and anger between the spouses turns into recognition and joyful reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The scene follows the Kural’s order exactly: a quarrel, its resolution, and coming together.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene, not checked verbatim this session; the quarrel-recognition-reunion sequence is a strong match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Amantium irae amoris integratio est” (The quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love).
philosophy.explanation: In Terence’s comedy a father consoles himself that the lovers’ quarrel he hears of will only renew their love.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in one line: the lovers’ sulk leads to a stronger reunion.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Latin line and line number confirmed on several reference sites (including Wikiquote); a near one-to-one match, from Roman comedy rather than formal philosophy.

kurals.tamil:
அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால் காமம்
செறிதோறும் சேயிழை மாட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aridhoru ariyaamai kandatraal kaamam
seridhorum seyizhai maattu.
kurals.meaning: The more one learns, the more one discovers how much one does not yet know; so too, each time I come close to my jewelled beloved, my love finds something new.
kurals.elementary: When you read one good book about space, you find out there are a hundred more things about space you never knew. The more you learn, the more there is to learn! The lover says love is like that: the more time he spends with the one he loves, the more new things he finds to love.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with a celebrated simile from learning: aṟitōṟu aṟiyāmai kaṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like discovering one’s ignorance each time one learns’), so is kāmam (love) each time he draws close (ceṟitōṟum) to the cēyiḻai (சேயிழை, ‘she of red, i.e. gold, jewels’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify learning from books (nūl), and Solomon Pappaiah reads the second half as love’s savour appearing ever new; Kalaignar likewise has ‘knowing new things again and again’. The verse links the Kamattuppal to the Porutpal chapters on learning (ch. 40-43), and turns the humility of the scholar into a picture of inexhaustible love. Pope’s second line slightly shifts the sense: ‘The more men learn, the more their lack of learning they detect; / ’Tis so when I approach the maid with gleaming jewels decked.’ The ytamizh.com ‘Couplet Explanation’ reads it as repeated union only creating desire for more, a narrower gloss than the Tamil commentators give. Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Kena Upanishad says that Brahman is truly known by the one who thinks he does not know it, and is not known by the one who thinks he knows it; it is unknown to those who know and known to those who do not.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that the highest reality always exceeds what one thinks one has grasped.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds that deeper knowing reveals how much remains unknown.
hinduism.source: Kena Upanishad 2.3 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; matches the knowing-and-not-knowing half of the simile, not the love half.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that whoever thinks he knows has not yet begun to know as he should.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural’s simile: true knowing reveals how much is still unknown.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); matches the learning image but not the application to love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘If the sea were ink for [writing] the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it in [continual] supplement.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that God’s words are inexhaustible, so that all the oceans as ink could never write them all.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s endless discovery, the Qur’an points to a depth that can never be reached by learning.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; shares the idea of the inexhaustible, applied to God’s words rather than to love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Bag Bag said: Turn it over, and [again] turn it over, for all is therein. And look into it; And become gray and old therein.”
judaism.explanation: The sage teaches that the Torah can be studied again and again for a lifetime and still yield new meaning.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s love, which finds something new at every meeting, is like the Torah that is never exhausted by study.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:22 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a good match for inexhaustible depth, about Torah rather than love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that knowing the extent of one’s ignorance is the beginning of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the learning half of the Kural’s simile: wisdom grows as one sees what one does not know.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the awareness of ignorance, not the love theme.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that sense-desire is never satisfied, however much it enjoys.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds joy in a love that is always new and never used up; Jainism sees the same endlessness as the misery of a desire that can never be filled.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the endlessness is shared, but valued in the opposite way.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus and Penelope are reunited, Athena holds back the Dawn at the edge of the Ocean and lengthens the night, so that the couple can share their joy and tell each other all that has happened.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess stretches the night because the lovers’ delight in each other has no natural end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s love, which finds something new at every meeting, is matched by a reunion so rich that the night itself must be lengthened.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; it shows inexhaustible delight but lacks the learning simile.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates concludes that his only wisdom is knowing that he does not know.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the classic statement of the first half of the Kural’s simile, the learner who sees his own ignorance.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (Jowett); a strong match for the learning image, not for its application to love.
